newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Dozens reported dead after Indonesian riot.
newsitem.headline: Dozens reported dead after Indonesian riot.

text.p: Searchers found 65 bodies in a gutted shopping complex after riots rocked the South Kalimantan provincial capital of Banjarmasin on Borneo island, the Indonesian armed forces spokesman said on Sunday.
"Our preliminary investigation...says that 65 have been found dead on the second floor," Brigadier-General Slamet Supriadi told Reuters in Jakarta.
He said 181 people had been arrested following the riots on Friday, the final day of campaigning for Indonesia's national and local elections next Thursday.
Security authorities believed the dead were rioters trapped by flames in a second-floor supermarket in the multi-layer Mitra Plaza shopping complex, he said.
The Indonesian-language Dinamika Berita newspaper in Banjarmasin, quoting the local police chief, said on Sunday 79 people died in riots, 75 of them in Mitra Plaza.
It said two people had died in another burned-out supermarket and two had died of stab wounds.
Dinamika Berita said 100 people were injured in the violence which swept the city of 400,000 people.
The violence erupted following clashes between supporters of the ruling Golkar party campaigning in the city and angry crowds emerging from mosques after Friday prayers.
Previously, most of the campaign violence had been confined to the main island of Java, primarily between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP).
The official Antara news agency said police had found "tens of scorched bodies" in Mitra Plaza, which was sealed off by police and troops.
Antara said its reporter had seen heaps of "scorched human skulls in three locations of the shopping centre".
Security forces guarded riot-hit areas of the city on Sunday morning, but elsewhere life was more or less normal.
Dinamika Berita said six government buildings, nine banks, two hotels, six restaurants and a number of shops and houses were destroyed.
Witnesses said smoke still rose on Sunday from a burned out Protestant church and a devastated housing area nearby, where the church caretaker said 500 families had lived.
The director of the Ulin general hospital, Dr Sudarto, told Reuters 69 people had been admitted to his hospital, of whom 30 were still being treated, mainly for broken bones and stab wounds.
At the hospital, Taiyibono, a 23-year-old motorcycle mechanic, said he had been on his way home on his motorcycle on Friday afternoon when he was caught up in the violence.
"I was going home when I was stopped by the crowd. They searched me and found a Golkar flag under my motorbike seat which I had used in the campaign a few days earlier.
"Then they hit me on the head without warning and slashed me with a machete. I ran before they could attack me again and someone brought me to the hospital," he said.
The father of a 13-year-old boy being treated for a broken wrist said he had not expected there would be any danger in the election campaign.
Junaidi said his son Tedy was wearing a yellow Golkar T-shirt when attacked.
"Children don't know anything about politics. The T-shirts had been given free in the neighbourhood and he borrowed it from his mother.
"Everything had been safe up until then, and as a parent I had no suspicion it would be dangerous for my children to join the campaign," Junaidi said.
